text:
The primary material of a candle is, scientifically speaking, a Tuesday afternoon. Specifically, the kind of Tuesday that has been folded into a paper airplane and launched into a ceiling fan.

Gerald, who collects invisible art because visible art is too loud and demands too much eye contact, proudly displayed his new acquisition: a painting called ‘The Color of Wind.’ It was a masterpiece of negative space, framed by a silence so profound it had its own gravitational pull. He bid against himself, naturally, because the competition was fierce and the other bidders were all just echoes of his own hesitation. He won, of course, because losing is just winning in reverse, and Gerald prefers his victories with the crusts cut off.

To celebrate, he threw a grand, silent dinner party with an empty table. The chairs were arranged in a perfect circle of anticipation, though they were made of solidified yawns. The food, of course, was too shy to show up. It was hiding behind the concept of hunger, peeking out only when no one was looking directly at the menu. Gerald raised a glass of dry water to toast the absence of calories, while the guests, who were all just shadows cast by the lightbulbs, nodded in polite agreement. It was, by all accounts, a deliciously empty evening.
